parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: For a progressive wave, state what is meant by

markscheme_points.text: time for one oscillation/one vibration/one cycle or time between adjacent wavefronts/points in phase or shortest time between two wavefronts/points in phase

hints: Hint 1: Picture one single particle as the wave passes - focus on how long it takes for its motion to repeat exactly once.
parts.proper_answer: The period is the time for one complete oscillation of the source, or of a particle in the wave.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Think in time at one place**
Imagine you stay at one fixed point and watch the particle there move up and down. A progressive wave makes each particle vibrate with simple harmonic motion.

Step 2: **Define the repeat time**
The period $T$ is the shortest time for that motion to repeat. That is the time for one full vibration, one full cycle, from e.g. crest to next crest passing you.

hints: Hint 1: Now freeze time and look along space - focus on the shortest distance over which the pattern of displacement repeats exactly.
parts.proper_answer: The wavelength is the minimum distance between two points oscillating in phase, e.g. between two adjacent crests.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Think in space at one time**
If period is repeat in time, wavelength $\lambda$ is repeat in space. Freeze the wave and take a snapshot of displacement against distance.

Step 2: **Define the repeat distance**
It is the distance the wave travels in one period, which is the minimum distance between two adjacent points that have the same displacement and velocity, i.e. are in phase.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Fig. 4.1 shows the variation with time $t$ of the displacement $x$ of two progressive waves P and Q passing the same point.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1

The speed of the waves is $20\text{ cm s}^{-1}$.
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the waves.
hints: Hint 1: From Fig. 4.1, look along the time axis for wave P and find the time for the pattern to repeat once, e.g. from one peak to the next peak.
Hint 2: Now link that repeat time to speed and wavelength using $v = f\lambda$ with $f = 1/T$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the period from the graph**
This is a displacement-time graph at one point, so the repeat in time is the period. For wave P, start at $t = 0$ going up, return to the same slope and displacement at $t = 0.60\text{ s}$. Peaks are at about $t = 0.15\text{ s}$ and $t = 0.75\text{ s}$. So $$T = 0.60\text{ s}$$ Both waves have the same $T$.

Step 2: **Use wave speed to get wavelength**
You know speed is distance per time, and in one period the wave moves one wavelength: $$v = f\lambda = \frac{\lambda}{T}$$ So $$\lambda = vT = 20 \times 0.60 = 12\text{ cm}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the phase difference between the two waves.
hints: Hint 1: Find the time shift between the same feature on P and Q, e.g. upward zero-crossings or peaks, and think what fraction of one full period $0.60\text{ s}$ that shift is.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Measure time lag**
A full cycle $360^{\circ}$ corresponds to one period $T = 0.60\text{ s}$. Wave Q lags wave P. For example P crosses zero going up at $t = 0$, Q crosses zero going up at $t = 0.20\text{ s}$. So time delay $\Delta t = 0.20\text{ s}$.

Step 2: **Convert to phase**
Phase difference is the fraction of a cycle: $$\phi = \frac{\Delta t}{T} \times 360^{\circ} = \frac{0.20}{0.60} \times 360^{\circ} = 120^{\circ}$$ $240^{\circ}$ the other way round is also correct.

key_concepts: time delay as fraction of period

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Determine $$\frac{\text{intensity of wave Q}}{\text{intensity of wave P}}$$.
hints: Hint 1: Read the maximum displacement (peak height) for each wave from the $x$-axis in Fig. 4.1 and think about whether intensity grows linearly with that height.
Hint 2: Recall the power law linking intensity $I$ to amplitude $A$, then form the ratio using your two amplitudes.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get the amplitudes**
Amplitude is the maximum magnitude of displacement. From the graph: $$A_P = 3.0\text{ mm}$$ $$A_Q = 2.0\text{ mm}$$

Step 2: **Apply intensity law**
For a wave of fixed frequency, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared: $$I \propto A^{2}$$ Hence: $$\frac{I_Q}{I_P} = \frac{A_Q^{2}}{A_P^{2}} = \frac{2.0^{2}}{3.0^{2}} = \frac{4.0}{9.0} \approx 0.44$$

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text: The two waves superpose as they pass the same point. Use Fig. 4.1 to determine the resultant displacement at time $t = 0.45\text{ s}$.
hints: Hint 1: At $t = 0.45\text{ s}$ draw a vertical line on Fig. 4.1 and read the two separate $x$ values carefully, watching the sign above and below zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Add displacements by superposition**
When two waves occupy the same point, the total displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements, keeping sign: $$x_{total} = x_P + x_Q$$

Step 2: **Read values at t = 0.45 s**
At $t = 0.45\text{ s}$, wave P is at its trough: $$x_P = -3.00\text{ mm}$$ Wave Q is on its way down from its peak: $$x_Q = +1.00\text{ mm}$$ So $$x_{total} = -3.00 + 1.00 = -2.00\text{ mm}$$
